title: One-to-One, and When It's Really Inheritance
description: A group of columns only some rows ever use is usually a second table waiting to happen. Model it as a one-to-one and the database can finally say "these facts arrive together or not at all". Why it matters: a wall of nullable columns is a rule nobody wrote down — and the database cannot enforce a rule it was never told about.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About

One-to-one is the rarest of the three relationship shapes, and the most misunderstood. When you genuinely need it, it is almost always for one of two reasons: a **group of optional attributes** that only some rows have, or a **subtype** — a kind of thing that is a special case of a more general thing.

Think of a passport. Every citizen has an identity record; only some have a passport. You would not staple four blank passport pages into every citizen's file just in case. You keep passports as a separate set of records, each one belonging to exactly one citizen.

## Scenario

Run this:

```sql
SELECT * FROM CustomerImport;
```

Six customers. Four are individuals; two are businesses. And four columns — `VatNumber`, `CompanyRegNo`, `TaxCountryCode`, `VatVerifiedOn` — are `NULL` for everyone except the two businesses.

Those four columns are carrying an unwritten rule: *either all of them are filled in, or none of them are.* A customer with a VAT number but no country code is nonsense. But nothing in the schema says so, so nothing prevents it:

```sql
UPDATE CustomerImport SET VatNumber = '4999999999' WHERE Name = 'Thandi Mokoena';
```

The database accepts that happily. It has no idea the group belongs together.

There is a second cost. Every one of those columns has to be nullable, which means you can never write `NOT NULL` on any of them — even though, for a business account, every one of them is genuinely required.

## Your task

Model this properly: a `Customers` table for the facts every customer has, and a `CustomerTaxDetails` table for the group that only business accounts have, related one-to-one.

`Customers` is already on the canvas. Add `CustomerTaxDetails`, connect it, and set the relationship's cardinality to **one-to-one**.

## What to look for

**A one-to-one is a foreign key plus a uniqueness guarantee.** That is the whole trick. A plain foreign key allows many child rows per parent — that is one-to-*many*. What makes it one-to-*one* is that the child's foreign key columns cannot repeat.

There are two ways to guarantee that, and the neater one is to make the child's foreign key **also its primary key**. `CustomerTaxDetails.CustomerId` is both: it identifies the row *and* points at the customer. A primary key cannot repeat, so a customer cannot have two tax records. (The other way — a separate surrogate key plus a `UNIQUE` constraint on the foreign key column — works identically and costs you an extra column.)

**Notice what the new table can say that the old columns could not.** In `CustomerTaxDetails`, `VatNumber` and `CompanyRegNo` are `NOT NULL`. The unwritten rule is now written down and enforced: a tax record exists in full, or it does not exist. That is the real prize here, not tidiness.

**This app derives cardinality rather than taking your word for it.** After your DDL runs, the schema is read back and a foreign key is reported as one-to-one only when its columns are actually covered by a primary key or unique index. Label a relationship one-to-one on the canvas without backing it with uniqueness and the check will disagree with you — correctly.

## The concept

When you see a one-to-one, ask which of these it is:

1. **An optional attribute group** — like this one. The child table exists because the facts belong together and only apply sometimes.
2. **A subtype** — `Vehicle` with `Car` and `Truck`, each holding the columns only that kind has. This is inheritance expressed in tables, and the child's shared primary key is what ties an instance to its general form.
3. **A splitting-for-performance decision** — moving rarely-read wide columns out of a hot table. Legitimate, but it is a tuning choice rather than a modelling one, and it should be made with measurements rather than instinct.

And one case where it is *none* of the above: if the child table's columns apply to every parent row and are always populated, the one-to-one is buying you nothing. Put them back. A relationship that is never optional and never repeats is just columns with extra steps — and an extra join.

## How this is graded

As always, the check runs your DDL against a real SQL Server and grades the schema that comes back, not the drawing. Writing the `CREATE TABLE` statements by hand instead of using the canvas passes identically.

steps.prompt: Add CustomerTaxDetails and connect it to Customers. Set the cardinality to one-to-one — and make sure the model actually backs that claim.
Generate and run the DDL, then move the six rows across from CustomerImport — the two business accounts get a tax record, the other four do not.

hints: The new table's key is not a new number. It is the customer's own id: CustomerId identifies the tax record and points at the customer at the same time.
Uniqueness is what separates one-to-one from one-to-many. If CustomerId is the primary key of CustomerTaxDetails, a customer cannot have two tax records — the constraint does the work for you.
Once the columns live in their own table, they can be NOT NULL. That is the point of the exercise: the rule 'these arrive together' becomes something the database enforces.
